newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mobutu to go home Friday, France readies troops.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu to go home Friday, France readies troops.

text.p: Ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko of Zaire plans return home on Friday to seek a political solution to his country's deepening crisis, his son said on Thursday.
Mobutu Nzanga, who is also his father's spokesman, told Reuters the president no longer ruled out talks with leaders of a revolt in eastern Zaire.

France, Mobutu's staunchest international backer, meanwhile announced it had sent aircraft and 100 troops to neighbouring Congo and Gabon in case it needed to protect or evacuate its nationals from war-torn Zaire.

"Given the situation, and in order to ensure the safety of our citizens if necessary, the Ministry of Defence has decided to sent extra resources to Libreville and Brazzaville," Defence Ministry spokesman Pierre Servent told reporters.

The 66-year-old president, released from a Monaco hospital on Wednesday after further cancer treatment, failed to appear at the last minute at a photo session called apparently to show that he was not seriously ill.
"He has a very busy schedule today so it will be very difficult to have a photo session this morning," his son said.
"He is going to the capital tomorrow. His intention is to find a solution to the present crisis in consultation with parliament, the government and the military high command," Mobutu Nzanga said.
He said Mobutu, facing a spreading revolt against his 32-year rule, did not rule out talks with rebels but would first discuss the issue with political leaders in Kinshasa.
"That is premature. It has to be done in agreement with the government and the parliament, which are the principal institutions of our country," Mobutu Nzanga said.
It was not clear whether a ceasefire remained a prior condition for starting negotiations.
The rebels' spokesman said on Thursday in Goma that if the international community wanted to halt fighting it must press Mobutu for direct negotiations.

They face heavy international pressure to stop fighting and negotiate a solution to the war. Long-time Mobutu opponent Laurent Kabila, who leads the rebels, demands direct talks with Mobutu, or someone appointed by him, before a general ceasefire.
Kabila's forces say they will only negotiate on how Mobutu, who seized power in 1965, stands down.

African leaders meeting in Nairobi on Wednesday with Zaire's prime minister called joined calls by the United States, the European Union, South Africa and France for a ceasefire to pave the way for negotiations to end six months of fighting.
The Zairean government has accepted a five-point U.N. peace plan, the first item of which is an immediate ceasefire.
But so far the rebels have agreed only to a ceasefire around the northeastern capital of Kisangani, which they captured last weekend.

Mobutu Nzanga declined to comment on an attempt by the transitional Zairean parliament to fire Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, saying the president would discuss it with the country's political institutions on his return.

"On that question, we have no comment to make because it is essentially the parliament's responsibility. As soon as he arrives, he will meet with the leadership of the parliament on that issue," he said.
